name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: An AI Gateway and Python SDK for Routing LLM Traffic
answer: LiteLLM is an AI gateway and Python SDK from BerriAI that lets you call over 100 LLM APIs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, in OpenAI or native format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It sits between your application and model providers, so a reader deciding whether to use it should know that the project is mid-migration from a Python proxy to a Rust core, and that the Rust gateway is still an early beta.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and published at github.com/BerriAI/litellm under a custom licence, with a Python SDK and a proxy server that the documentation calls the fastest, litest AI Gateway. The repository shows a last push on 3 October 2026 and about 60,000 stars. It occupies the gateway layer of the AI stack, sitting between application code and model providers. Rather than calling each vendor SDK directly, you point your code at LiteLLM, which normalises requests into OpenAI format or passes them through in native format, then handles routing, authentication, budgets, rate limits, logging and cost attribution. The official site describes one control plane spanning an Agent Gateway, a Model Gateway and an MCP Gateway, so the same layer that routes model calls also governs agent invocation and tool access.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs are model routing and failover across providers, cost tracking and spend attribution, guardrails, load balancing, logging, and centralised key and budget management. The documentation shows reliability testing across providers with batch_completion_models_all_responses, which sends one conversation to every model in parallel and returns only the responses that succeeded, and load_test_model for concurrent request testing. It is strongest where a team runs several providers or several business units against shared models and needs one place to enforce budgets, rate limits and access. The Agent Gateway authenticates callers, records request, response, latency and cost data, and forwards verified user and team context to agents as X-LiteLLM-User-Id and X-LiteLLM-Team-Id. The MCP Gateway centralises tool access and upstream authentication, including per-user OAuth with auth_type oauth2 and oauth2_flow authorization_code. It is not a training framework, and the site does not present it as one.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for anyone comfortable with Python and HTTP APIs, since the surface is largely OpenAI-shaped calls with a model string. The harder parts are operational rather than mathematical: understanding proxy deployment, Redis, database-backed budgets, Kubernetes behaviour and provider quirks. No mathematics prerequisite appears in the material. The official site offers tutorials, a blog, incident reports and reference documentation, including a tutorial on testing multiple providers and pages on identity and FinOps. A beginner can follow the tutorials, but the incident reports show that running the proxy in production demands attention to version pinning and upgrade discipline, which is a systems skill rather than an AI one.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The facts list integrations with Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, and the description claims over 100 LLM APIs. The documentation describes an A2A JSON-RPC interface for invoking shared agents, an Admin UI where agents appear with status and spend data, OIDC authentication, SSO and SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails. LiteAdmin MCP lets an agent handle tasks through the gateway's management API, and LiteAdmin, a Slack admin agent, was built on the same connector. The blog carries tags for ai-gateway and incident-report, with 12 and 14 posts respectively, which is unusually transparent for a project of this size. Community size is indicated by the roughly 60,000 stars, though the facts do not give contributor counts or release cadence beyond the dates mentioned.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: It is built for both, but the two halves are at different stages. The Python SDK and proxy are the mature path, and the blog states the Python proxy peaks around 359MB of memory under load, with per-request overhead around 7.5ms. The Rust gateway is an early beta that the blog says serves about 15x the throughput, 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11x less memory, 359MB to 32MB, and cuts per-request overhead to about 0.05ms, against a commitment of sub-1ms overhead and a sub-100MB binary. The stated goal is a pure Rust server serving 100% of traffic with auth and rate limiting in Rust. The cost of that is migration risk: the Rust path is beta, and the Python path is the one with the incident history and the version-specific fixes.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The material shows enterprise use, including an enterprise customer running litellm-database:v1.100.0 behind nginx, and features aimed at platform teams such as SSO, audit logs, multi-team management and per-team budgets. The blog reports a benchmark against Portkey, Bifrost and the current LiteLLM Python proxy, and claims the Rust gateway has the lowest p99 added latency and smallest memory footprint of the four, roughly 7x lower overhead and 9x less memory than Bifrost. That is a vendor-run benchmark, so treat it as directional. The project is a current choice rather than a legacy one, given the 2026 release activity, but the incident reports show that operating it well is a real skill. For someone choosing what to learn, gateway and FinOps work around LLMs is a growing area, and LiteLLM is one of the visible tools in it.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is written in Python and used from Python, and it sits in front of provider SDKs rather than replacing them. The documentation notes it calls Mistral's API directly over HTTP via httpx and does not import the mistralai Python SDK anywhere, which is the same pattern it uses for other providers. It is typically deployed alongside a web framework or agent framework that makes the calls, with Redis for caching and rate limiting and a database for keys, budgets and spend, and it exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint so existing OpenAI client code can point at it unchanged. The polyglot pattern is a Python application or agent talking to a gateway that speaks to many providers, with the gateway itself moving toward a Rust core while keeping the Python SDK as the developer-facing surface.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The incident reports are the clearest statement of weakness. A Medium severity incident caused a production outage for one customer in September 2026, with kernel OOM kills, one worker reaching 61GB RSS and thousands of 502s, triggered by unbounded retry breadcrumb growth when a provider kept failing and Redis was unreachable; the fix was not backported to v1.100.0 before it was tagged stable. A separate Medium severity incident silently broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock in v1.91.0 and v1.91.1, dropping cache hit rates from roughly 90% to 25-45% and raising spend 2-3x with no error surfaced. The blog also notes that server-side Claude Code auto mode depends on a contract some gateways did not preserve, LiteLLM included, with a fix shipping in the stable release planned for 3 October 2026. The classifier benchmark comparing TypeSafe JEV with Haiku is explicitly qualified as dependent on the prompts and tier definitions used, authored with synthetic prompts and without independent review. The official material does not state a support policy, a long-term release cadence, or how complete the Rust migration is beyond the early beta, and the custom licence is not explained in the pages read.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
